title: Playing the same parts each time; vamping bass licks
summary: Dutcher asks whether parts are the same each time on Maryland. Ridgley describes vamping bass-violin-style figures, sometimes higher.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: Well, let's say that today was the day that we worked out for the first time in Maryland, my Maryland, and then you worked out the parts that you were going to play, and you'd probably play five or six choruses, the band would total, seven or eight choruses, and you had that all worked out. When you started playing it, would you play the same notes pretty much every time in the weeks and the months as they went by? That you worked out that first day in Maryland? That trombone solo? Well, no, not just the solo, but all the back parts and everything that you were playing.

Yeah, you see, outside of that solo, most of the time, someone like used to vamp his way through, you know, like a bass violin, you know, and he'd make him say, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, you know, all those kind of stuff like that. And then if it could go high, you'd sing or something like that, some of that would go low, you know, but most of them that would be this style, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, and then make him.
Would you do that in higher registers too? Yeah, you could do that in higher registers too?
Yeah, you could do that in higher registers. Yeah, it could sound good. Do you try to do it up? I could do it, yeah. Well, I never was a real high one, but I couldn't make B-flat, you see.
See, I could sing B-flat, I could sing B-flat then slightly.
